utterances.text: No, I didn't hear any noise from aeroplanes. The night the tanks came, the whole population woke up and left. It was early in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm not asking you this. Could you please answer my questions. We've already heard that from you. You provided that in your statement; you also said it in the Milosevic case.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Well, I'm saying here what I heard and what I experienced; I'm not saying anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krasniqi. During that same night, did you hear a loud powerful detonation, a loud explosion? I'm not asking you about any tanks. I'm asking you about an explosion.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: There was no explosion in my village that night, nothing. I didn't hear any explosion.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions for this witness, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I do have some questions. One moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise. I would like to tender the photo into evidence, and can the photo be given a number. I apologise to my learned friend Ivetic for interrupting his examination.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be IC73, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Krasniqi. My name is Dan Ivetic and I am one of the attorneys for Mr. Lukic in these proceedings. I have a few questions for you today, and I would ask you to please focus on my questions to give the most concise and accurate answers as possible. Now, first of all, sir, in your village of Krusha e Vogel, how many ethnic Serbian inhabitants were there in the village as of March 1999?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Could you repeat that again. I couldn't hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sure. With respect to your village of Krusha e Vogel, how many ethnic Serbian inhabitants were there in that village as of March of 1999?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Albanian inhabitants? Oh, Serb inhabitants. I don't know. There were 23 households, but how many of them there were altogether, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. You state there were 23 Serb households. Is it accurate that there were about a hundred Albanian households?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: No, there weren't a hundred Albanian households.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise. A hundred Albanian houses. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Not a hundred Albanian houses. At that time there were about 70.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, would it be accurate to state that these Serbian inhabitants of the village consisted of several extended families, such as the Nikolics, the Petkovics, the Stankovics, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Their families, immediate families that they had there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What I'm trying to say is these were larger-sized families, extended families. There were many brothers and --

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Only a few members.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Is it accurate to state that prior to March of 1999, specifically prior to the commencement of the NATO air-strikes, you and the other Albanian villagers had not experienced any violence directed toward you or against you?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: No, we never had any problem with the Serbs. I had my neighbour there who was a Serb, and I never had any problems with him. I don't know why they did what they did that day, that massacre. We would never expect that to happen. We never expected that from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now you've explained --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you ask that. You refer to a neighbour who was a Serb. What was his name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ranko Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, that shortens my cross by one question, Your Honour. You're ahead of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Krasniqi, first of all, did anyone else in your village change their last name like you did?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I'm focussing about -- I want to focus on the surrounding area around your village, the surrounding villages. Is it accurate to state that there were some so-called KLA forces in the surrounding area, particularly in some of the surrounding villages around Krusha e Vogel in 1999?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: In 1999, we didn't even dare to go up the mountain, we the people of Krusha e Vogel. We didn't dare because of the Serbs, because there were Serb forces in the village. We couldn't go to the forest. I personally did not go to the forest to get firewood for the winter. So that winter we went to the market and bought firewood; we couldn't go to the forest.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, I thought you had told me that prior to the NATO bombings you had not had any problems with the Serbs. So I don't understand why you would be afraid of moving due to Serbs being there.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Because they thought ill of us, and we didn't dare go to the mountains for that reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right. Well, then, let me ask you a question focussing on your village in particular. Do you know whether there were any persons in your village who were members of the KLA at the time, that is to say, any time from 1998 up until the commencement of the NATO bombings?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I did not see anything with my own eyes. People spoke about things and they said that there were KLA somewhere else, but not in my village. I'm positive about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And did people also speak -- or did you have any knowledge of any kidnappings by the KLA or attacks by the KLA, either in your village or in the surrounding area?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: KLA existed in Kosova, but there was no KLA presence in my village at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Did you have knowledge of any kidnappings or attacks by the KLA in the surrounding -- area surrounding your village?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I heard that they were fighting with the army, but nobody was kidnapped from our village. Not even from surrounding villages. I never heard of such a thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I would like to know leading up to the NATO bombings, that is to say, before the NATO bombings began, did you and others in the village hear media reports or otherwise the fact that there was the potential for NATO action against Yugoslavia? Were you able to hear about that or know about that in your village in the days prior to the commencement of the NATO bombings?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I never read newspapers. I don't follow the news. I mind my own business. I work.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. What about the other villagers? Did anyone else in the village talk amongst themselves about the potential that war would come between NATO and Yugoslavia over Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I didn't hear anything about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Was there any type of fear or tension among the villagers, either the Serbs or the Albanians, in the days preceding the NATO attack?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Not in the village, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, another question about the Serbian villagers in your village prior to March of 1999: Is it accurate that many, if not most, of the able-bodied Serb male villagers wore remnants of some kind of uniform, either a blue camouflage uniform or some other uniform and colour?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, because people saw them, the Serbs, in the village in uniforms; army reservists uniforms and other kinds of uniforms. They kept changing their clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And when did that start, approximately? Was it long before March of 1999, close to March of 1999? Do you have any time reference for that?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: It was in 1998 that we saw them, that they were wearing various kinds of uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And now with respect to those persons in your village wearing these various types of uniforms, is it accurate to state that they were employed in regular jobs, that is to say, that their profession did not involve being full-time police or full-time army?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, we saw them. I'm sure they did some kind of job, or maybe they were unemployed. I did not see them working anywhere. I saw them in uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I want to ask you specifically about the ones that were wearing police uniforms, and ask you if, in fact, it is accurate that you do not know what their formal affiliation, if any, with the police was.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Well, they went somewhere in those uniforms. I did not ask them where they went.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did they drive around in private civilian cars rather than marked police cars? Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And you indicated that these Serb civilians in your village began wearing uniforms in 1998. Is it accurate that they also had guns in addition to the uniforms?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes. They were seen carrying guns. I saw them myself in 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And yet prior to March 25th of 1999, these armed villagers, in various uniforms in your village, did not undertake any attacks upon you or the other ethnic Albanians in the village. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: No. No, not in the village. Not a single villager was attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, I'd like to ask you some specific questions about some specific persons in your village. You talked about a gentleman by the name of Dimitrije Nikolic. Is it correct that he operated a cafe in your village, by profession?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And was --

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, it was a cafe and a pool parlor. They stayed there all the time. There were policemen. There were people in multi-coloured uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, is it correct that -- strike that. Is it correct that the Nikolic family had a large number of members that resided in Krusha e Vogel?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes. There is one family with several members; I don't know how many.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And this Dimitrije Nikolic, is it accurate that he worked at this cafe in the village of Krusha e Madhe, more or less on a daily basis? I'm sorry, Krusha e Vogel.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: In his cafe, yes, of course, he was the owner of that cafe. His son worked there as well. And all the policemen went there in uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: When you say "all the policemen went there in uniforms," are we talking about the local villagers in police uniforms?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: No, no. Others. We didn't know them at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in your statement from 1999, you state that on the night the NATO air attacks began, all the Serbs turned off their lights and you saw your neighbour went into the basement with his family. Did you have the impression that people in your neighbourhood were concerned for their safety as a result of the NATO planes flying overhead?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I don't know what they were thinking, whether they were frightened, or what the reason was why they went into the basement. I just know that I saw them going into the basement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you know about Albanian households? Did they turn off their lights or go into shelters in the basement?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I didn't see the Albanian families. I, myself, don't have a basement, so I stayed where I was and I kept my lights on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Had you had a basement, would you have gone in it?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: For what reason? There was no reason for me to go in the basement. The NATO forces were not dealing with families.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in your 1999 statement, you also talk about how, on the morning of the 25th of March, 1999, your household and other Albanian households went to hide in the forests and mountains. I want to ask you: How far were these mountains and forests from, let's say, your home?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: In the outskirts of the village. I've not measured the distance. Some ten minutes on foot. There is a road there that takes you to the mountain.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And do you recall what time of day that was? Was it light out or was it still dark out?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: On the 25th of March, it was dawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And you state further in your statement that at that time the village started being burnt and that this continued into the next day. Now, from the distance that you were at, could you personally see who was burning the houses in your village?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: No, no. We were far away. We could only see the smoke coming out from the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And, in fact, do you know the percentage or number of houses in the village that were burned on this day, in this manner?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: We did not see how many houses were burned on the 25th or the 26th of March. We couldn't see any of that. Nobody was thinking of the number of houses that were on fire. Everybody was concerned with their own families and themselves, whether they will survive or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I appreciate that. I appreciate that and it makes sense. Now, did you have an opportunity to see whether, in fact, all the Albanian families left the village for this forest area on the morning of 25 March 1999; that is to say, in this area where you were located, did you see any families that were not there, that were distinctly not there?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes. There was part of the village that fled in the direction of Drini.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you know if any of the Albanian families remained in the village that day and even the next day, the 26th of March, 1999?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Not a single family remained in the village on the 25th or 26th of March. They cleansed the village of all the villagers.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the Hajdari family, Isuf and his family?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether they left the village on the 25th of March, 1999?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Nobody knew whether he fled the village on that day with his family or if he was killed or if he was burned. We only knew about the people who came to the outskirts of the village in the mountains. This is how I learned that not all the villagers had escaped to the outskirts of the village in the mountains.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, going onward with this 1999 statement, you state at this time, while you were in the forest area, you saw MUP policemen taking away vehicles and tractors. Now, first of all, I want to ask you: How could you see that it was policemen who were taking these things?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: You could see their uniforms. They had police uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: From that distance, could you identify whether these persons in those uniforms were, in fact, local villagers from your village or not?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I could not identify what they were. Of course there were local villagers as well, together with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you go on to state that at that time 15 policemen came into the forest where the people were hiding, and you saw -- according to your statement, you saw three policemen with white ribbons tied around their arms giving instructions. Now, I want to ask you: What kind of uniforms were these three persons with white ribbons wearing so as to permit you to conclude that they were policemen?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: They had all kinds of clothes, all kinds of uniforms. They had ribbons around their upper arm. They would issue orders. What should I call them?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, what I'm trying to differentiate is whether everyone had these white ribbons tied around their arms or whether there were only certain individuals in particular who had the white ribbons tied around their arms.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Some of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And if I can perhaps refresh your recollection, you gave a statement to the ICTY on 5 October 2001 wherein you stated that the persons with the white ribbons tied around their arms were, in fact, paramilitaries in green camouflage uniforms. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes. As I said, they would change uniforms. They always changed uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And in your March 7, 2002, addendum statement you further clarify that these particular three paramilitaries with the white ribbons tied around their arms also had yellow bands on the left side of their chest. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And now the 15 policemen that you said came there, did these 15 individuals wear the same uniform, or did they also have a variety of uniforms on?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Some had the same uniform; some had other uniforms. Not all of them had the same uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, who directed the women and children to go to Albania at this point in time, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Those who were there told the women, "You can either go and drown yourselves in Drini or go to Albania."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you personally hear these words?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, I personally heard these words.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Were they spoken in Serbian or Albanian?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: In Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And did you recognise the voice of the speaker?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I heard his voice, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm asking, did you recognise the voice as someone you knew?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, was it the same people in various uniforms that forced you to kneel, said NATO would rescue you soon, and then escorted you to the house of Haxhi Batusha?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: We didn't know them. We had our hands above our heads. We were kneeling down. We didn't even dare look at them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I need a little bit of clarification as to where you were taken. In your statement, you reference someone -- that this was the home of -- the house of Haxhi Batucha, that's H-a-x-h-i, last name, B-a-t-u-c-h-a, but I have reason to believe that you've also referred to this location as the house of Razim Batusha. Which is the correct identity of the person who's house this was?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Rasim Batusha is Haxhi's father. Rasim Batusha was in Germany, but we called his house Batusha's house. Rasim Batusha is now at home, while Haxhi Batusha is missing, together with 28 members of his family.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And so we're talking about just one house. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, it's the same house.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And is this the house where you and the other persons from the village were led and where the shooting occurred? A. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is there also a person called Qazim Batusha?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The grandfather of Haxhi Batusha.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, for clarification purposes during the direct examination this structure was referred to as a barn or cowshed, whereas in your written statement throughout it's referred to as a house; and, in fact, now we've been talking about it as a house. What, in fact, was this structure?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: When it was built, it was a two-room house with a corridor. When we were taken to that house, a part of it had hay inside. The part where I was, on the right side, it had hay inside. So that's why we called it a barn and sometimes a house. But, to me, that's not important. The important thing is that people are missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Just one more question about that structure itself. Did the windows -- were the windows finished; that is to say, did the windows have glass in them, or were they open?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: There were windows but no glass.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And you already testified in direct that Shefqet Shehu called out to one of the local Serbs from the village who was there, and then that the shooting started and continued until he was out of bullets. Do you know how long, approximately, the shooting lasted? Was it just this one -- this one individual shooting, or were there multiple persons shooting? And how long did the shooting last?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: After they executed the people in that room, Shefqet Shehu was lying down. He stood up. They did not call for him to stand up and be executed, but he thought that they were no longer there. He wanted to escape. But this Serb from the village happened to be there at the window. So when Shefqet saw him, he said to him, "Neighbour, you are doing this?" And then he started shooting again. But I cannot tell you the exact time, how long this firing lasted.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. That's fair enough. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, just hold on. Were you able to tell at all whether there was only one person shooting or whether there was more than one person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my room there was only one person who was shooting through the window.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And after -- at some point in time the individuals there from the village started a fire by throwing stuff on the bodies, and you were there inside the structure at the time. Do you have any more specific of an idea of how long you were in this burning structure, more specific than what you stated in your statement that you had been pushed into the house at about 1100 hours and escaped at about 1500 hours? Can you narrow down that four-hour span of time to tell us how long you were in there after the fire had started?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: After the fire started, all of us who were injured were blocked by the fire. When they threw this hay on the bodies, the smoke came down and then I stood up and decided to go outside and rather die from a bullet. I did not pay attention to how long I stayed there. That was of no interest to me because of what was happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And when you left that structure and went to your uncle's house -- first of all, how far was your uncle's house that you escaped to? Where was it located?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: From my uncle's house, there was only this narrow path that I took when I jumped off the window, and I went to the basement of my uncle's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And your uncle's house is in the adjacent lot next to the Batusha house. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Next to the house where the execution was carried out and where these men were burned.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in your original statement from 1999, you stated that you thereafter saw two policemen who added more corn/maize to the fire to feed the fire, but today you said that these were actually villagers from your village who did this, although you could not recall whether you saw persons in uniform. I'd like to refresh your recollection with your statement dated the 7th of March of 2002, which is also entered in evidence, where you state corrections to your original statement, and you say: "As concerns the placing of dried maize stocks on top of the dead bodies, I wish to make a correction. This was done by two Serb civilians called Slavisa Petkovic and Ljubisa Stankovic, who were not wearing police uniforms. I know them very well as we used to sell vegetables together in the market." Do you recall identifying the people who added the corn/maize to the fire as being two individuals from the village that you used to sell vegetables together with?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: When I left the cowshed and went to my uncle's house's basement, after that I climbed on the second floor. And from there I could see the stable of Krasniqi, and the dried cornstalks from there were thrown on the bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: By these two civilian villagers from your village, Petkovic and Stankovic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, I saw both of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, do you recall making a handwritten statement in 1999 sometime after you returned from Albania wherein you identified the persons who took part in all the crimes you saw and testified about in Krusha e Vogel on the 25th of March and the 26th of March, 1999?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I don't know. Maybe I did, but I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, I would ask the court officer to put up on e-court Exhibit 6D89. The first three pages of that exhibit are the English translation received from the Office of the Prosecutor. I would ask that the fourth page of that exhibit be placed on the e-court for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, if you could look at the screen. Do you recognise this handwritten document and --

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- do you remember writing it?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And do you remember writing it as well?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And if I can direct your attention to the next page in e-court, the second page of the handwritten document. First of all, sir, do you recall when, in fact, you wrote this document?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: No, I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. But do you recall turning it in to the international authorities that were in Kosovo at the time?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. If you look at this page that's up on the screen now, there is a list of some persons. In fact, you list some 37 persons by name, labelled as "Serb War Criminals of Krusha e Vogel," and then there are three persons who are identified as being sons of number 26 on that list without any names for them. Are these all the local Serbs from your village, that is to say, neighbours of yours?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And are these all persons who participated in committing crimes against you and others in your village on the 25th and the 26th of March, 1999?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I didn't see them taking part in that. But as for Momcilo Nikolic, that, Shefqet saw, and I heard from Shefqet that he participated in the execution. I've seen Dobri Petrovic's -- Petkovic's sons with weapons in their hands on the 25th of March, 1999, in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, do you recall -- while you were in Albania, do you recall giving an interview to someone from either the OSCE or the International Crisis Group?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I don't know to whom I was giving the statement. Maybe I did give to this organisation, but I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, then, just let me ask you a general question that hopefully you will be able to answer. Do you recall giving an interview to anyone in Albania wherein you described that, while you were watching what was going on in your village that night, you saw certain of the persons involved, the perpetrators, injecting drugs by way of a small vial, smaller than a cigarette lighter, into themselves?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: No, I don't remember these as being my words.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. I have a few more questions for you. In your village, is there a small bridge that goes over a river?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: A stream? On both sides of the village there is one.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So there's a total of two bridges and they cross a stream rather than a river. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, above the streams.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And is one of these bridges near the entrance to the village, that is to say, near the main road Prizren-Djakovica?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: The main Gjakova-Prizren road, there are two bridges over that road. No other bridges.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I am talking about bridges crossing a stream or some other body of water. Is there one that is near the entrance to the village from the main road? And when I say "near," I don't know the actual distance, so it might be a little bit further away. But is there one that is closer to the entrance to the village than the other bridge?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, on the main road Prizren-Gjakova, between the villages of Krusha e Madhe and Krusha e Vogel. If you're asking about the entrance to the village, I think that's the bridge you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Is there a bridge towards the Drini?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: No, not towards the Drin.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. On either the 25th of March or the 26th of March, 1999, was there any fighting that you were aware of around the area of any of the bridges in your village between the members of the KLA, on the one hand, and Serb forces, on the other hand?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did any of the bridges, in fact, become damaged during the war; that is to say, did any of these bridges in the village appear to be damaged when you returned to the village from Albania?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Not in Krusha e Vogel, not even in Krusha e Madhe. The bridge between the two villages was not damaged, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krasniqi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krasniqi, we have to interrupt now for the break at lunchtime. You should --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I'd just make a suggestion. [Interpretation] My questions for this witness have been exhausted, actually, but he did raise a topic on page 49, lines 17 to 25, and I would like to put three or four questions regarding that. Now, I don't know how to deal with it. Can I do it now? Or would you allow that to happen in the first place? Should we just leave it for later?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, I'm happy, as long as it's fairly brief, Mr. Visnjic. Carry on and see how you get on, then. Mr. Krasniqi, it looks as though we could finish your evidence, possibly finish it, if we continue just now before our lunch break, so Mr. Visnjic will ask his questions now. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Krasniqi, today you said that in 1999 you could not go to the mountains, that is to say, the inhabitants of Mala Krusa, and that inter alia you, yourself, did not go into the forest to get firewood because you were afraid of the Serb forces that were in the village. Mr. Krasniqi, is it correct that in the forests above your village there were members of the KLA in the winter of 1999?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: No. I never saw anyone. We just didn't go there because we didn't want the Serbs in the village to think ill of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, do you know a person by the name of Cvetko Nikolic from the village of Mala Krusa?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: No, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, will it perhaps jog your memory if I tell you that on the 27th of February, 1999, above the village of Mala Krusa, members of the KLA abducted Cvetko Nikolic; and after this kidnapping they took him to an illegal KLA prison in the village of Randobrava, also in the municipality of Prizren? Mr. Krasniqi, how far away is Randobrava from your village? Isn't it about 2 kilometres away?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: It's far away. I don't know how far away exactly that is. I can't tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Do you know about any one of the Serbs from your village being abducted in February 1999?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: We heard about these things, but it was not a kidnapping. I did not go and ask people about this, but as far as I could hear, that was not a kidnapping because he returned home immediately. I don't know the name of the person. I don't know if you mean the same person that I have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, I'm referring to Cvetko Nikolic who was abducted by the KLA and freed through the good services of the OSCE monitoring mission from the regional monitoring centre in Prizren. Cvetko Nikolic, otherwise a retarded man.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I don't know whether he was retarded or not. I don't know what he was doing in Randobrava. I don't know. I couldn't tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: He was in the forest, Mr. Krasniqi, and he was abducted and taken to Randobrava.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Your Honours. My foundation for this is a document provided by the Prosecution. It's in EDS 01383968. It's not in the system because the witness raised the subject only today. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Visnjic. Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honours, two questions, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, you were asked in cross-examination about the Nikolic family, the family of Dimitrije Nikolic. And at some point you said that his son was also working in this cafe in your village. What is the first name of this son, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Cvedan Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And do you know, did he have any other sons? And what were their names?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: He had another son as well, but I can't remember his name now.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: That's all, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, Mr. Krasniqi, that completes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal again to give it and to add to the evidence you gave before. You're now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And we shall resume at 2.15. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.39 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I gather you want to say something, Ms. Moeller?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, if I may from this position. I would like to tender two more exhibits from the bar table from the witnesses we heard yesterday and today. One is Exhibit P2333, which is a request for assistance from the Tribunal to Serbia and Montenegro, requesting information on names, and the second document is the response to this request, which is Exhibit P2335. These documents contain names which were the subject of the testimony of the two witnesses we heard, and I would therefore like to tender them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You have had copies of them readily available, or do we have to see them on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: I don't have paper copies now, Your Honour. If they could be brought up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Of this document, if we could go to page 3, please, and scroll down a little.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And the response?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: The response is Exhibit P2335, page 2, please. If we could have the English attachment. It's the same page, also page 2 on the English version. If Your Honours wish, I can provide a reference to where these names appeared in the evidence that was adduced in the past two days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Not necessary at the moment. Thank you. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We have an objection to the introduction of this document on several grounds. We had noted our objection yesterday when this document was first attempted to be used with one of the other witnesses, and particularly with the testimony we heard today, it's very clear that this document lacks the type of probative value that would make it admissible and useful for our purposes. For instance, the very first individual on this list, Dimitrije Nikolic, the information that is provided here obviously is not for the Dimitrije Nikolic that the witness testified relative to, who he said was a full-time cafe owner in Krusha e Vogel. This information is for an individual in Urosevac, which is quite a far distance away from Mala Krusa. In fact, if you look at the JMBG numbers, I'm told, in my crash course of the Yugoslav system, that there is a sequence of numbers in there that can tell you where, that is to say, from what portion of the old Yugoslav state, the individuals hailed from. The several individuals that have 95, which would be the Prizren municipality, but there are several individuals here who have numbers which indicate they do not hail from the municipality where this village is located, and therefore we can't be certain that these are individuals that were testified to or might be other persons. As he indicated the other day, these names are fairly common names and therefore it appears to us now that what was done was that the request was made to Serbia and Montenegro and they just did a search within the MUP database for anyone with name without regard for the precise location as being sought. So based upon that, without further information, this documentation is of little probative value. And I submit that the harm or prejudice could be great if, in fact, someone on here is mistaken as being one of the persons that was testified to, which, again, with the few individuals that we did hear about - at least number 1 on the list, Dimitrije Nikolic - this is clearly not the man that was being testified to by the witnesses, who both said that he had a cafe there. And I believe the witness today testified that that Dimitrije Nikolic worked daily in his cafe in Mala Krusa. So I don't know how he could simultaneously be working daily in his cafe in Mala Krusa and also be the assistant shift supervisor of the SUP in Urosevac, which is quite a few kilometres away. It's several municipalities removed. So on that basis, we would object to this document because we cannot verify any of the information as being directly related to the persons that were testified to, at least in this form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And the others all appear to be within the Prizren office?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Actually, they don't. Number 20 is from Urosevac; number 25 is Pristina --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: They may not be names that it's sought to refer to. Which ones do you seek to refer to, Ms. Moeller?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honours, we seek to refer to a number -- a couple of these names. Mainly where -- all the persons that, according to this information, belong to the SUP prison. Number 2, Svezda Nikolic; number 3, Sava Nikolic; number 4, Momcilo; number 5, Ranko; number 10, Novica; number 13, Borislav Cvetkovic; number 19, Zlatko Djordjevic; number 23, Dejan Petkovic; number 25, Goran Petkovic. He is here said to belong to the SUP Pristina, but I think on the basis of this information, and that applies equally to Dimitrije Nikolic, it is not clear that the information contained herein excludes the possibility that they may, indeed, be the same persons. And we think it goes to the weight of the document. And we also have requested additional information on these individuals but we have not received any response yet. Such information will be made available as it comes in. And I'm certain that the Defence will also in their case have the opportunity to investigate all these individuals further --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: -- and present material.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's precisely my point; that, absent additional information, this document is not reliable, especially given the fact that some of the individuals they want to make reference to are listed as being totally different persons in a different reason. Now, even with the persons that are within Prizren, I don't know how many Nikolics there were. We saw today a list of -- I think it was 37 persons, of which I think 15 were Nikolics just in that one village. There might be more in Prizren; it's a pretty large place. I have no way of knowing whether these are, in fact, the persons from this village absent any additional information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We will admit the request P2333 and we will admit the response insofar as it relates to the various officers identified by Ms. Moeller, with the exception of numbers 1 and 25. We exclude them on the basis that there's nothing in this document that would indicate they were the persons serving within the Prizren area, and in particular in Krusha e Vogel at the relevant time. Now, that doesn't exclude the possibility of the Prosecution supplementing this document by further information as the result of their inquiries. But those that clearly indicate that they fell within the jurisdiction of the Prizren area we will admit. We accept that there is an argument about weight and whether, in fact, that establishes anything in particular. But taken with other evidence in due course, it will be weighed and a decision taken about whether it assists us ultimately to determine the identity of the personnel involved in the incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I would only add, then, that I think for context and the full record --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, would you kindly slow down for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I will slow down for the interpreters. For the completion of the record and for context, I think we should also include the other individuals for which it says the MUP has no information about this person, since I believe those were also names that were on the various lists in the witness statements by these witnesses and were submitted by the Office of the Prosecutor relative to this event. And that, therefore, might also have some value in weighing the evidence and the identifications that are made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is there any objection to that, Ms. Moeller?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: We would object to the extent that not all the names in this document were actually addressed with the witness, and we would ask the Defence to identify the names which were addressed with the two witnesses. Where it says the MUP has no information, we would not object to these names being entered as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I could -- I could prepare a list and present it to Your Honours so as not to take up more time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you content in principle with the point that's made, that it should be confined to those who were named?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I agree, I agree in any of the evidence. I would make one more point. Number 9 is also an individual from the OUP in Kacanik. I don't know if that was one of the ones that the Prosecution had wanted to have admitted or not, but the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't think it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If it is, I would say that that one should also be excluded. I don't have it in my notes, so I don't know if it was listed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Moeller, can you clarify that one?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: We had included that name in the list because it was issued today when the document was addressed by Defence counsel. Yes, we still argue, because the witness has said that also policemen they didn't know from their own village were present, that this may be one of the persons. But it's up to Your Honours, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that's a very thin argument, because there would be no basis on which either of these witnesses would have identified the officer. But number 5 was not one of the numbers you gave us -- number 9, rather, was not one of the numbers you gave us.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: I thought it was, Your Honour, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You went from 2 to 5 and then to 10, 13, 19, 23, and 25, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes. That's fine, Your Honours. We will maybe come back to that point if we obtain more information for this particular person. But for the time being, this is -- yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: For the avoidance of doubt, number 9 is not included in those that will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And as I said, we will submit a list of the other ones after looking at the various transcripts so as not to waste more court time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, yes, the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. DRAGULEV
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, the next witness is Edison Zatriqi. The witness's evidence was originally proposed under Rule 92 bis (B), but he's now being called under the new Rule 92 ter. His testimony is relevant to the municipality of Pec and in particular to paragraphs 72(e) and 77 of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So we're embarking on a new chapter now, Ms. Dragulev, are we?

utterances.speaker: MS. DRAGULEV
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Zatriqi.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you please make the solemn declaration to tell the truth by reading aloud the document which will now be placed before you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Now, Mr. Zatriqi, we have your statement before us, but you are here so that you can answer questions that counsel will put to clarify things in the statement, perhaps to add to them, and perhaps to challenge some of the things that you've said. And the first counsel to ask you questions will be for the Prosecution, Ms. Dragulev. Ms. Dragulev.

utterances.speaker: MS. DRAGULEV
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. DRAGULEV
utterances.text: Mr. Zatriqi, could you please state your full name and spell your first and last name for the record.

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: My name is Edison Zatriqi.

utterances.speaker: MS. DRAGULEV
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please spell your first and last name.

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: Yes. E-d-i-s-o-n, Z-a-t-r-i-q-i.

utterances.speaker: MS. DRAGULEV
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zatriqi, did you provide a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor dated the 20th of June, 2001?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DRAGULEV
utterances.text: And did you make a correction to that statement on the 29th of January, 2002?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. DRAGULEV
utterances.text: And have you had an opportunity to review those two statements during our proofing session yesterday?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: Yes. I reviewed them and read them.

utterances.speaker: MS. DRAGULEV
utterances.text: And are your two statements true and accurate, to the best of your knowledge and recollection?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely true.

utterances.speaker: MS. DRAGULEV
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. DRAGULEV
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to tender Exhibit P2347, which includes the witness's statements dated the 20th of June, 2001, the addendum to his statement dated the 20th of -- 29th of January, 2002, and his signed 92 bis declaration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. DRAGULEV
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. DRAGULEV
utterances.text: Mr. Zatriqi, I would like to move to the events that occurred in Pec on the 27th of March, 1999. Did you see any armed people on that day?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: On that day I saw many armed people in my neighbourhood, people in uniform and civilians that were carrying weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. DRAGULEV
utterances.text: And the people in uniform, what colour was the uniform that they were wearing?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: The uniformed people, their uniforms were blue, camouflage, combined blue and black colours.

utterances.speaker: MS. DRAGULEV
utterances.text: Thank you. And the armed civilians, did you know any of them?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: Yes, I knew most of them because they were my neighbours, who were civilians but they were armed. And they were moving around.

utterances.speaker: MS. DRAGULEV
utterances.text: And what was the ethnicity of those neighbours?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: These neighbours who were armed were of Serb ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MS. DRAGULEV
utterances.text: Thank you. And you stated that you left Pec on the following day, the 28th of March, 1999. Why did you leave Pec on that day?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: I left Peje because the Serbian police expelled us from our homes, so we were forced to leave our homes and our town.

utterances.speaker: MS. DRAGULEV
utterances.text: And how did they expel you?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: On Sunday, which was the 28th of March, I was not at my home, I was in another house, in another neighbourhood, and a policeman went from home to home telling people to leave their homes, and gave them a maximum of five minutes to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would kindly ask my learned colleague from the opposite to point the part of this statement where this witness stated so.

utterances.speaker: MS. DRAGULEV
utterances.text: Your Honour, we provided a supplemental information sheet yesterday, and that information was contained in that. It's also -- we also referenced the transcript in Milosevic --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The Milosevic transcript is not part of this package, as I was informed.

utterances.speaker: MS. DRAGULEV
utterances.text: That's correct. But in the supplemental information sheet, we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The objection I think, though, Ms. Dragulev is to the question which was -- well, sorry. No. I think it followed an earlier question. What exactly is your objection, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Part of the package is actually a combination of these two statements, and in those statements we cannot find any kind of mentioning of police officers expelling those people from their homes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And it's not part of 65 ter motion as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Well, that's a different point. What's the answer to that? It's not been intimated as evidence that will be led from this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. DRAGULEV
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was -- as I said, we provided a supplemental information sheet yesterday, and it was mentioned in paragraph 9 of that supplemental information sheet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The summary of the evidence that the witness is likely to give includes the statement: "The witness states that he left in fear of his life." And, in view of the intimation made yesterday by "supplemental information sheet," then we consider that simply to be an elaboration of that part of his evidence that was heralded in the 65 ter summary, and therefore we'll allow the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. DRAGULEV
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. DRAGULEV
utterances.text: Mr. Zatriqi, the policemen who came to your house and gave that five-minute ultimatum, did he wear a uniform?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: Yes, he was in uniform, the same uniform I described earlier; camouflage, blue camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. DRAGULEV
utterances.text: Thank you. And you stated that you then joined a convoy of vehicles. Could you please briefly describe that convoy.

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: Yes. After we left the house, we joined the convoy in the road parallel to the one where we were living. There was a very long convoy with cars, but also a column of people, a very long column of people, walking.

utterances.speaker: MS. DRAGULEV
utterances.text: And did you stay with the convoy until you reached Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: Yes, I was in this car convoy all the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. DRAGULEV
utterances.text: Mr. Zatriqi, you stated that your buses had been taken away from you by policemen. Did you see any of your buses while you were driving in the convoy?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: After I joined the convoy, at the first crossroads, which was 100 or 200 metres away, I saw one of my buses full of people. The driver of the bus was wearing a blue camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. DRAGULEV
utterances.text: Were the people on the bus armed?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: No, no. They were people from my town who were being forced to leave, and they had been loaded on the bus.

utterances.speaker: MS. DRAGULEV
utterances.text: And did you see any other buses while you were driving in the convoy?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: Yes. In addition to my bus, there were other buses which were confiscated from my colleagues, and they were packed with citizens.

utterances.speaker: MS. DRAGULEV
utterances.text: Thank you. Page 3 of your statement states that you saw armed policemen at various road junctions who were directing you towards Montenegro. Did those armed policemen wear uniforms?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: Yes. At the first junction where we were led to by the police -- the police there were wearing the same uniform and they were armed.

utterances.speaker: MS. DRAGULEV
utterances.text: My last question, Mr. Zatriqi, relates to your return to Pec on the 26th of July, 1999. You stated that your house had been burned and your office buildings and your buses had all been burned. Did you see any other houses in the village that had been burned?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: When I returned to Peje, I saw many houses that had been burned and destroyed in addition to my own house.

utterances.speaker: MS. DRAGULEV
utterances.text: And do you know who those burnt houses belonged to? Do you know the ethnicity of the people the houses belonged to, the burnt houses?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: Yes. All of the houses that had been burned and destroyed were Albanian houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. DRAGULEV
utterances.text: And did you see any houses -- any burnt houses that belonged to Serbs?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: No, I didn't see any. The houses that I knew Serbs were living in before, those houses were not damaged.

utterances.speaker: MS. DRAGULEV
utterances.text: And did you see any mosques or religious sites that were damaged or burnt when you returned?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: Yes. I saw many, for example, mosques and other buildings. But there was this Qarshia Xhamia, which was under the protection of UNESCO, it was completely destroyed. The red Xhamia in Kapeshnica and other religious sites as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. DRAGULEV
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The witness also mentioned Hamam Xhamia.

utterances.speaker: MS. DRAGULEV
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zatriqi.

utterances.speaker: MS. DRAGULEV
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: The order shall be: General Lukic, General Pavkovic, General Ojdanic, Mr. Milutinovic, Mr. Sainovic, and General Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Zatriqi. I'm Branko Lukic, and I will have a few questions for you today. We've had a very busy schedule this week, and I must admit that this is the first time I've seen the supplementary material provided to us by the OTP in relation to your testimony. You mentioned today that a policeman came to your home, or rather, to the house where you were staying, and that he said to you that you should leave that house. Was the policeman alone?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: In the neighbourhood where I was staying, before I answer your question, this neighbourhood has two entrances or two exits. And on these two entrances there were police cars, two police cars stationed. And the policeman who came to tell the occupants in the houses to leave was alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know the policeman?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were there many policemen from your town that you didn't know?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: Of course there were. Of course I couldn't have known every single one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did this policeman talk to you personally?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: No, he didn't talk to me personally, but from the way he moved and walked, it showed us clearly that we had to leave the houses, all of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So he didn't talk to anyone from the house where you were staying?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: It is true that he didn't talk to anyone, but he addressed us collectively.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll go back to that, but now I'm going to ask you about something else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'd rather clarify it now, I must say, if you don't mind, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's not clear to me what this policeman did to convey the message to you that you had to leave. Could you explain that to us. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's very simple. He walked along the road of that neighbourhood and told the population that we should leave the houses. This was an activity that came two days after some major shellings and other activities that they performed. So it was very obvious for us that we should leave the houses. Near the house where I was, there was this hill and you could see that the police was coming down that hill. And that's why it was a reason for us to collect the families, to gather them all together, and leave to a safer place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you tell us his tone of voice and what he said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The tone was very high, and he said that we should leave the houses in five minutes, max.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you please tell us in what part of town you were on that day, on the 28th of March?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: Yes. On this day I was in the Jarina part of Peje.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You owned a company before the war. How many employees were there in the company?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: Yes. I was the owner of the Flamingo Tours company and it had a total of around 17 employees.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you have any employees who were Serbs?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: No. No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On the police force, did you have any friends? Because, by virtue of the fact that you were involved in this line of work, one would think that you would have friends on the police force.

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: I wouldn't say that I had a friend or acquaintance, but -- however, whenever I needed something, I had acquaintances there. But not friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So you turned to them for different favours; right?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: I wouldn't go to them. We would meet somewhere or meet on the street. But these were for just some minor things, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On the 23rd, when they came and they asked for your buses -- or rather, what you say here is, on a particular day in March in 1999 -- but if I understand things correctly, it would have to be the 23rd, because you say it was definitely the day before the start of the NATO bombing. So can we say that it's the 23rd of March, 1999?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: It should be so, because it was just one day before the NATO air-strikes began. But the police came to my house. They asked me to go to the place where the buses were -- in fact, they wanted me to move the buses from there because they needed that space. I hid myself. They spoke with my mother. And later, then, I went to the place where they required my presence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you went to that particular place, you came across Bulatovic and Misljen; right?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: Yes. I met Bulatovic and Misljen there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know these two men from before?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You asked them for a certificate stating that your buses had been taken; right?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: Yes, I did, because they asked me to start the engine of each one of the buses, and after I did so, they told me I could leave. So, for me, it didn't make sense, leaving the buses with the engines on and not having any certificate. That's why I asked them to issue me with a certificate that these buses were taken away from me, and to state the reasons there why they were being taken away from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After that they threatened you; right?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: Yes, you can consider it a threat; that it was no times for certificates, it was time for calibres. And when they mentioned calibres, it was very clear to me what they meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After that you did not go to the SUP to report the incident; right?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: No, I didn't go to the secretariat to file a complaint because Misljen was deputy commander of the police, while Bata Bulatovic was an inspector. Therefore, I knew that even if I go to report it there, it won't be to any benefit whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did they say anything as to what they needed these buses for?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: No, they didn't say anything. From the moment I started the engines, they said that I was free to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you ever have any personal conflicts with these two men?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know when your buses were torched?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: I returned relatively later. But from the information I collected from people and from my colleagues, it was sometime just before the Serb forces withdrew from Peje. That's when the buses were destroyed and burnt.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that at the moment when the Serb civilians were withdrawing from Pec, there was a major shortage of vehicles? What am I trying to say to you? Don't you think that it's illogical, at the moment when as many vehicles as possible are needed, that buses are torched and then civilians have to walk?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: As I said earlier, I returned relatively later, and I don't know of these movements of the Serb population that you're putting me. What I know is that in addition to my three buses, about another ten were also burnt. So in total, about 15 buses were destroyed and burnt.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You don't know who burned the buses, right?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: No, I don't know the name and last name of the persons who did that. But based on the information I got from my friends and colleagues, they were destroyed by the Serbian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You say that you did not have any problems during the journey, that you drove straight to Rozaje. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: Yes, you can say that. Except for some provocations along the road, we didn't have any major problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So the policemen that you saw during that journey did not attack you, did not shoot at you. Can we conclude that they were trying to regulate the traffic, the traffic commotion that was there because of so many people being on the road?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: No, we can't say so. It is true that there were policemen on crossroads, but they were not there to regulate the traffic, as you are saying. They were giving us directions. For example, I could not go right or straight on a crossroad, but to the direction that the policeman was showing me; in my case, the direction towards Rozaje.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So they did not direct you to go towards Albania or Macedonia; they were directing you to go to Montenegro. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. They were directing us to go Montenegro on the left side of the city, that is, people coming from the left side of the town; while people coming from the right side of the town were directed to go to Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Montenegro and Serbia were a single state at that time; right? So this is just my last question at this time for the sake of formality. The Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, that was the name of the state at the time; right?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zatriqi. Thank you for having answered my questions. I have no further questions for you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I was just going to say "No questions," Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm just anticipating.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't have any questions either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: No questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I will now disappoint you. I have a couple of questions. Maybe three.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Zatriqi, I'm Mihajlo Bakrac. I will just follow up on the last question put to you by my learned friend. You said that you returned in July of 1999, if I'm not mistaken, and you were in Rozaje all that time before you returned. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: No. I was in Turkey during this time, in a town near Antalya.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Zatriqi, when you returned -- or rather, you told us about the buses, that you had received information from your friends and colleagues. Were those friends and colleagues Albanians, the ones who told you about your buses?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: Yes, all of them were Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And those are the Albanians that remained in Pec; that's how you were able to obtain information from them. They were in Pec all that time. They did not flee, like you did.

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: All these colleagues left Peje, indeed. Some of them who lived on the right side of the river, they went to Albania, while the others who lived on the left side of the river, to Montenegro. Once they returned after the NATO forces entered Kosova, they were informed by the people who lived near the place where our buses were parked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think that's the point Mr. Bakrac is making to you. There must have been people who stayed in Pec, and they would be the ones who saw your buses being burned.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course there were citizens who were unable to leave. My colleagues, however, who had their buses confiscated, they did not stay in Peje either. They got this information from the people whose houses were near the place where the buses were parked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes. But let's be very precise. Those people whose houses were in the vicinity, they are Albanians, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: Yes, Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: When the international forces entered Pec, were there any Serbs left; and also when you returned to Pec, were there any Serbs left there?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: As I said, I returned relatively later. There were Serbs in our town, but they were stationed at Peje's Patrika.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And my last question to you, Mr. Zatriqi, is this: When you provided your first statement on the 20th of June, 2001 - and we have it here - the reason for your departure stated therein is this: "We left because there was shooting going on all night." That was the reason that you provided. You didn't say then that anybody had told you to leave. How come you've changed that in the meantime?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: I did not change my opinion at all. You can see from my statement that the gun-shots that were heard throughout the night were heard from my house. And the following morning, together with my family, I moved to Jarina neighbourhood, to my aunt's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And now you've explained your reasons for departure. Thank you very much, Mr. Zatriqi. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Dragulev.

utterances.speaker: MS. DRAGULEV
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, please. I just want a little explanation. What do you mean by "Peje Patrika"? What is this place? Or why is it called "Peje Patrika"?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: This question is for me, Your Honour?
