utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: It's an Orthodox church in Peje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Oh. Thank you very much. And were these people confined there when the forces came within the church compound, the Serbs I mean, when the forces came?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: I wasn't there when the NATO forces entered Peje, but when I returned, I saw that there were Serbs at the Peje Patrika.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I mean, that was a place where they were all made to assemble, or they were there already, or you saw some of them there? Thanks.

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: I don't know the reasons because I wasn't there when they moved to the church. But you can see the road that goes to Rugova and you can see that there were people going to this monastery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: How many you saw?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: When I happened to pass by there about two or three months after the NATO forces entered Kosova, I could see about 30 to 40 people from the road.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zatriqi. That completes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it. You're now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, I hope you're dreading the next question, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have no more witnesses for this week. We lost one that we thought we were going to have. I know we cut it pretty close to the edge. But since next week we had no court planned, I made my best estimate. Some of the cross-examination went faster than I expected, and I hope the Court won't be too disappointed in the fact that we covered a lot of territory this week, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think it can be said you did extremely well in your planning for this week.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But I did indicate informally yesterday that it might be a suitable opportunity to review progress. Can you help us on how we're doing and how this fits in with -- how the progress fits in with your original estimate of the time that you would like to take to present your case?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, it's hard to say, because in these beginning months, Your Honours, we have focussed on crime base, and a number of our witnesses have been 92 bis witnesses and are shorter than a number of our upcoming witnesses. By my calculations, I think today, now, Your Honour, we have, counting the one 92 bis (C) witness, whose testimony you admitted, Mr. Russo, I think we now have evidence from 49 witnesses out of our approximately 170 or so on the list. So we're something more than 25 per cent but less than 30. However, as I said, we have our bigger, longer witnesses coming up, with the internationals, the experts, and some of the higher-level insiders. But I think we're progressing fairly well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And, of course, the rule change has given you the greater flexibility than you had before to use the provisions of what's now Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. And we have tried to take onboard some of the suggestions you've made and pointed out in terms of trying to do some things farther in advance with witnesses rather than just the day or two before they get here. We're just taking our initial steps to try and do some of that, using the facilities that you've pointed out to us that are available for such purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Looking broadly at the picture, you originally estimated 280 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour, but that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let me finish. We then took some of the crime sites out, which might have been said to reduce the estimate, but we then refused your application to have 92 bis witnesses without cross-examination. You, however, took the view that you should nevertheless examine these witnesses. But laying that little -- that part of it aside, perhaps the two developments that I've just summarised might be seen to have cancelled each other out, and we're probably back where we started.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I haven't done a precise calculation, but you may be right. The one may offset the other. I haven't sat down to do the math again --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And, of course, all of that is in the context of what you would like to have to present your case.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: One thing you mustn't lose sight of, no one here must lose sight of, is that certainly in the early stages of the trial we've used a very high proportion of time in matters which are not direct -- well, non-presentation of evidence. Hopefully that's -- well, it has reduced, and hopefully it will continue to take up a smaller proportion of the time. But it is quite disturbing to see, when you look ahead, just how long it might take to present a case, using the starting point of 280 hours. I take it you've worked that out?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. And so just finally, on the sitting times themselves, a number of views have been expressed informally that this has been a rather demanding week. Do you have a view to express on behalf of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, personally, Your Honour, I feel rather knackered, if I can borrow that expression. But I don't know, it's hard to explain. In America, in my system, we used to do jury trials from 9.00 to 5.30 on a regular basis, but I was younger then. And there's something about -- just this whole process. Maybe it's the nature of the cases, the translation, the additional pressures. But it has been a very tiring week. But we did -- I think we did accomplish a lot during this week. I don't know that I would volunteer to do it every week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, I understand that. But you make the point that I was going to make myself; that I'm not used to working 9.00 to 5.30, but I know that in the United States it's regularly done. And, therefore, it didn't seem to be out of the way. I also accept what you said about the process here, apparently making more demands on the individual. It may be something to do with the slow progress that's associated with translation, e-court, documents coming up, and so on. You'll get -- sorry --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, I didn't mean to interrupt you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'll come to you in a moment --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- Mr. Sepenuk. But you'll find that over the next few months and into the first couple of months of next year, there may be the facility for repeating what we've done this week because of cases being at judgement and their evidence having finished. And I must say, I certainly find it more civilised to sit in a way which allows you to concentrate for a morning and an afternoon and have a break in the middle of the day, rather than these -- confining it all to one part of the day. That doesn't mean to say we need to sit for all the hours that we've sat here, nor that we need to do it every day or indeed every week. But we've got to try to make use of the time that's available. Three and three-quarter hour days are not going to achieve -- exclusively, three and three-quarter hour days is not going to achieve, for this case, a resolution of the case within what strikes us as a reasonable time in the overall context. So there has to be, I think, imaginative use of available time. And it may be that by working longer hours at certain times, that other times there can be breaks which might be productively used out of court. An example, I hope, is what we've decided to do at the recess, at the Christmas recess. And there could be other opportunities along the way. Now, Mr. Sepenuk, you want to comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Well, as a matter of fact, Your Honour, in light of what you just said, I've decided not to pursue -- I was going to talk more about the American experience, but I'd rather the Court wonder why I didn't speak than why I did. So I'll leave it at that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, I know that there are counsel who do have views on scheduling, and I'm happy to hear from any who do. Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, if I can speak quite candidly about the situation this week. It appears to me that the Trial Chamber -- I hope the Trial Chamber doesn't lose its perspective on the impact of working a week like this. There is -- in a full day there's very little time for preparation and virtually no time to sit and reflect on where we've gone, what's happening this week and what will happen in the weeks to come. That's a very important consideration, I submit, in a trial like this. This isn't a two- or three-week matter. This is a lengthy matter. Many pieces have to fit together both in anticipation of how we proceed, how we prepare our Defence cases, which are coming. That requires time. The other factors are distance in this case. We have people in the region; we have potential witnesses who are on different continents. This is a leadership case. I hope the Chamber doesn't lose sight of those aspects, because this week wasn't very pleasant and there was virtually no time to reflect on what we're doing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: One of the things we have been bearing in mind is the long term, because we're conscious of the issues you mentioned. We're conscious of the fact that witnesses who will be coming that will take much longer to deal with than we've been dealing with so far, which will be much more important, possibly, than the ones we've been dealing with so far in relation to the real issues in dispute in the case. We have to bear in mind that there are six accused all to present defence cases if they wish. There has to be time for that to be organised and then for it to be presented. So it would be foolish to fail, I think, to take advantage of the time that can be used when these issues don't directly arise, albeit that may put certain demands on personnel, but we're in a very unusual situation, in an unusual environment, with a distinct job to do. So I recognise what you say, but if it's not every week, then perhaps the concerns you have can be addressed. And also if there is going to be a facility for interrupting it from time to time, then that may also address it. Overall, though, before I think we can plan sensibly ourselves, we may need to, at least in relation to the Prosecution case for the moment, think of applying overall guidelines or limits so that we can see just what the implications are of any requests that are made to sit at particular times or to adjourn at particular stages. It's interesting, I think, to also reflect that by giving guidance in advance of this week and by perhaps taking quite a tough line with the Prosecution on the way in which they had organised their witnesses, there has been a distinct improvement in the sort of efficiency of the trial process; however, I'll be the first to acknowledge that efficiency isn't the be all and end-all in this game. There is something that we have to bring to bear in this organisation which has so few resources. Now, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Hesitantly, I will speak about this again. Your Honour, the only thing that made this week possible for us was because the witnesses tended to be talking about minimal things, things that weren't of great high import, and especially for those of us who were not representing police, it was a -- it was a week that became manageable. But I hope you will understand that if we're sitting from 9.00 to 5.30, we really have no other time to work except from 7.00 until midnight, and that's what we have to do. And, you know, if you imposed those kinds of hours, from 9.00 to midnight, on the rest of the staff of this Tribunal, you'd have an immediate revolt, you'd have a claim of inhumanity, and all kinds of things like that. So you have to understand that that's what you do when you sit from 9.00 to 5.30; you put us in a situation where we work 15 hours a day. That's burdensome and it's oppressive and I think it's almost inhumane. If this was a two-week trial, like the United States trials you're talking about, nobody would object. But we're looking to try and stay in this kind of a schedule for as long as two years, and it's just not possible. It can't be done. And I don't know how to emphasise it further. Now, we were not able to do anything in terms of reviewing materials that we haven't reviewed yet, in terms of trying to prepare our own case, and things like that. We weren't able to do any of that this week. That's what we do with those mornings that we're not in session or those afternoons that we're not in session. We work on the witnesses that are coming; we work on preparing our own case. We do the stuff that's important to make this case work. We can't do it if we're sitting here from 9.00 to 5.30 every day. It's not possible. When I say it's not possible, you may say to me, "There are two or three of you working on this. Why can't one of you come to court and the other one do this work?" That doesn't work. We have to work, all of us, on witnesses to be able to do it. This week we had to substitute another counsel at this table to get through the week. As it turned out, it wasn't as important as I thought it might be. But it could have been and it could have been a serious problem. So this proposition that we should sit any time between 9.00 and 5.30 ever again is not acceptable in this kind of case. As I say, if this was a two-week trial, no problem, we could have been ready when it started; we could sit 9.00 to 5.30 every day. We do it in the United States. Not usually 9.00 to 5.30; it's usually 10.00 to 5.00 or something like that. But in any event, we do put in those kinds of hours. But they're cases where we have had time to prepare them, they're short in duration where you've got maybe 15 witnesses, and you're done. That's a whole different thing from having 170 witnesses and having to prepare a defence case in a case of this magnitude. So, as I've said before, if you let us do our jobs, we'll get this case done in a reasonable amount of time, efficiently. But if you put us under this kind of pressure, we're going to have serious problems. Some of us are just going to fall over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I have only two things to say about that. One is, with a trial as lengthy as this, there is an opportunity along the way to put right anything that might appear to be going wrong, which you don't necessarily have in shorter cases. The second thing I only mention because you've raised it, and others, no doubt, will have heard it. But I assure you there are dedicated young people working behind the scenes in this Tribunal who do work the hours that you have said would result in revolt; that perhaps not as obliged as somebody sitting in court, as a result, nevertheless, they do actually and, I dare say, would not like to be classed as rebels but the opposite.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I think that the -- I say this with some levity, that the operative word in what you just said was "young."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, just before we -- before we conclude, does anyone -- sorry -- yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Just briefly, as one of the younger persons here. I must admit our team is a little jealous to hear that some of the other teams actually got to bed at midnight. Our average sleeping time was quite a bit past that; I think the past several days, it's been about 4.00 in the morning. I have to stress that, especially when it -- when the witnesses have a particular focus on a particular defendants, this becomes quite onerous to prepare for each witness, especially when it -- as it happened this week, where one witness unfortunately drops out at the last minute, that really puts us in a crunch because we're only preparing for the witnesses as we go because of the lack of time. So we really were in a crunch when the one witness dropped out. We had to scramble to make sure that we were adequately prepared for however many witnesses might come in a given day. And it's been quite exhaustive and we got through it. But I just don't know how we can guarantee that we would have the same capabilities in the future, especially once we take into account the cumulative effect of fatigue and just the sheer number of documents involved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you have a list yet for a week on Monday?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We just received one I believe yesterday -- we just received the list today, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, the only other question I was going to ask was whether anyone on the Defence side does want to comment on time. I think that you used less than the maximum time for cross, around I -- in fact, all of the Judges consider the cross-examination was far more focussed since that guidance was given, and it doesn't appear to have lost anything in effectiveness. If we set guidance or time-limits, then it may be that the starting point is equality of time; but I think we recognise there may be occasions when there's a significant reason for there being inequality. So if there should be an order issued over the next few days, it will include the provision that, on good cause being shown, these limits will be varied.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: The only thing that occurred to me this week was the 14 witnesses that testified this week, it was somewhat arbitrary in the sense that I could imagine 14 other witnesses where there would have been rather extensive cross-examination, and I think that's what you've just told us. But as things evolved this week, the cross-examinations were more focussed for a variety of reasons. But I don't know if you could say that for every 14 witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But I think you can look back and say that, over the piece of the trial, it wouldn't have been much different, I think, if the cross-examination had been as focussed as it was this week. There were no -- I can't think of any particular examples where significantly longer would have been required generally for any of the crime base witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just briefly I would like to present another aspect of the problem that we have been facing. This week we had a number of witnesses who came from a number of different municipalities. For every municipality we have a certain number of documents that we have to overview and we are talking about a large quantity. So if the witnesses come so fast from different locations, we face a problem of trying to locate the adequate documents. In this respect, we have been either fortunate, or unfortunate, to have very few usable documents that we could use for our cross-examination. What is going to happen in the coming weeks is that the number of documents that the Defence teams are going to be using will grow in numbers, as the crime base witnesses draw to an end. In that respect, I'm going to -- I would like to try and draw attention to the fact that we will have problems with translation of some documents, and I would like to beg for your tolerance and your indulgence in allowing us to present the shortest documents in their original without their full translation, or maybe only as draft translations. Those documents are only in the possession of the Prosecution, and we will not surprise them with any of those documents. As far as I know, we have not been able to receive translations for two or three weeks, even if we insisted on them. But the witnesses are being announced seven days in advance, which puts a lot of pressure on us. And the only realistic option for the time being is for the Trial Chamber to allow us to use some of these documents, or at least some of passages from certain documents, in their original because we won't have the time to translate them fully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where the passages are fairly short, there's no problem about putting them on the e-court and having them translated as they are read. It's not the way things are supposed to be done, of course, and if it causes a problem for one of the parties, then that will have to be addressed. But it does seem a way around what could otherwise be a difficulty if there is a log jam with the CLSS translation. I'll certainly inquire about the situation and see if anything can be done to assist you. But I'm happy if short passages are dealt with that way, if you've failed, for good reason, not to get them translated in time. Draft translations should, I think, be discussed with the Prosecutor before they're used, if possible. And if the Prosecution are satisfied with the general standard of draft translation, then you might get over that. But initially, I think, you should be discussing the quality of what you produce unofficially. I think it also important when you're using documents to cross-examine that you have them well-prepared. The system is actually quite slow, as we're discovering, and efficiency of your preparation will assist in speeding it up. Anyway, thank you very much for -- oh, sorry, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just briefly, Your Honour. I'm looking at the transcript, and if anybody reads it, they may believe that I have been happy with the working hours, which would be the last thing I would wish to say. Thank you very much. This is my remark at the end of today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Bad move I would say, Mr. Bakrac. Right. Well, at least next week you'll be able to work 12-hour days. It will be a great improvement for you from what's happened this week. I hope you make the most of the time off and -- off from court sittings. We will resume at 9.00 on Monday, the 9th of October.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
